claim: Antibiotic-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Ng) are an emerging public health threat due to increasing numbers of multidrug resistant (MDR) organisms.
source: Antibiotic-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Ng) are an emerging public health threat due to increasing numbers of multidrug resistant (MDR) organisms.
evidence: This is a statement about the public health significance of antibiotic-resistant Ng, drawing from established knowledge about antibiotic resistance trends.

claim: PTC-847 and PTC-672 are novel orally active inhibitors that exhibit a narrow spectrum of activity against Ng including MDR isolates.
source: We identified two novel orally active inhibitors, PTC-847 and PTC-672, that exhibit a narrow spectrum of activity against Ng including MDR isolates.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing MIC values and selectivity testing.

claim: The class Ia ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) is a new therapeutic target for gonorrhea.
source: By selecting organisms resistant to the novel inhibitors and sequencing their genomes, we identified a new therapeutic target, the class Ia ribonucleotide reductase (RNR).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from resistance selection and genome sequencing.

claim: Resistance mutations in Ng map to the N-terminal cone domain of the α subunit of RNR.
source: Resistance mutations in Ng map to the N-terminal cone domain of the α subunit, which we show here is involved in forming an inhibited α4β4 state in the presence of the β subunit and allosteric effector dATP.
evidence: This is supported by genome sequencing data and structural analysis.

claim: The N-terminal cone domain of the α subunit is involved in forming an inhibited α4β4 state in the presence of the β subunit and allosteric effector dATP.
source: Resistance mutations in Ng map to the N-terminal cone domain of the α subunit, which we show here is involved in forming an inhibited α4β4 state in the presence of the β subunit and allosteric effector dATP.
evidence: This is supported by negative stain EM data showing α4β4 formation.

claim: PTC-847 and PTC-672 inhibit Ng RNR.
source: Enzyme assays confirm that PTC-847 and PTC-672 inhibit Ng RNR and reveal that allosteric effector dATP potentiates the inhibitory effect.
evidence: This is supported by enzyme inhibition assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Allosteric effector dATP potentiates the inhibitory effect of PTC-847 and PTC-672 on Ng RNR.
source: Enzyme assays confirm that PTC-847 and PTC-672 inhibit Ng RNR and reveal that allosteric effector dATP potentiates the inhibitory effect.
evidence: This is supported by enzyme assays showing enhanced inhibition in the presence of dATP.

claim: Oral administration of PTC-672 reduces Ng infection in a mouse model.
source: Oral administration of PTC-672 reduces Ng infection in a mouse model and may have therapeutic potential for treatment of Ng that is resistant to current drugs.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo efficacy data in mouse models.

claim: PTC-672 may have therapeutic potential for treatment of Ng that is resistant to current drugs.
source: Oral administration of PTC-672 reduces Ng infection in a mouse model and may have therapeutic potential for treatment of Ng that is resistant to current drugs.
evidence: This is speculative based on the in vivo efficacy data and activity against MDR strains.

claim: There were 78 million Ng infections worldwide with 90% of infections in low- and middle-income countries according to WHO, 2012.
source: They reported 78 million Ng infections worldwide with 90% of infections in low- and middle-income countries.
evidence: This is cited from WHO, 2012 report.

claim: In the US, during 2017–2018, the rate of reported Ng infections increased 5% (583,405 US reported cases in 2018 from CDC, 2019a).
source: In the US, during 2017–2018,, the rate of reported Ng infections increased 5% (583,405 US reported cases in 2018 from CDC, 2019a), and the rate increased among both sexes, in all regions of the US, and among all ethnicity groups.
evidence: This is cited from CDC, 2019a report.

claim: The rate of Ng infections increased among both sexes, in all regions of the US, and among all ethnicity groups.
source: In the US, during 2017–2018,, the rate of reported Ng infections increased 5% (583,405 US reported cases in 2018 from CDC, 2019a), and the rate increased among both sexes, in all regions of the US, and among all ethnicity groups.
evidence: This is cited from CDC, 2019a report.

claim: Ng was reported to be the second most prevalent notifiable sexually transmitted infection in the US (CDC, 2019a).
source: Ng was reported to be the second most prevalent notifiable sexually transmitted infection in the US (CDC, 2019a).
evidence: This is cited from CDC, 2019a report.

claim: The CDC currently prescribes a two antibiotic protocol using ceftriaxone (a β-lactam) and azithromycin (a macrolide) for Ng treatment.
source: Based on reported resistance of Ng strains, the CDC currently prescribes a two antibiotic protocol using ceftriaxone (a β-lactam) and azithromycin (a macrolide).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of CDC treatment guidelines.

claim: PTC-565 is a broad spectrum DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV inhibitor targeting Gram-negative pathogens (Gerasyuto et al., 2018).
source: The [5,6]-fused regioisomer (PTC-565, A) is a broad spectrum DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV inhibitor targeting Gram-negative pathogens (Gerasyuto et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from Gerasyuto et al., 2018 and shown in Figure 1.

claim: PTC-847 is a potent class Ia RNR inhibitor selective for Ng.
source: The [5,4]-fused regioisomer with a basic dimethylamine group appended to the indole C-2 (PTC-847, B) is a potent class Ia RNR inhibitor selective for Ng.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing selectivity and inhibition.

claim: PTC-672 is a selective Ng class Ia RNR inhibitor.
source: PTC-672 (C), a second selective Ng class Ia RNR inhibitor, has an imidazolyl moiety fused to the 4-hydroxy-2-pyridone through a seven-membered ring.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing selectivity and inhibition.

claim: RNRs catalyze the de novo conversion of the nucleoside diphosphates adenosine (A), guanosine (G), cytidine (C), and uridine (U) (collectively NDPs) to deoxynucleoside diphosphates (dNDPs).
source: RNRs catalyze the de novo conversion of the nucleoside diphosphates adenosine (A), guanosine (G), cytidine (C), and uridine (U) (collectively NDPs) to deoxynucleoside diphosphates (dNDPs) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about RNR function.

claim: RNRs are essential in all organisms for DNA biosynthesis because of their role in controlling the relative ratios and amounts of dNTP pools.
source: RNRs are essential in all organisms for DNA biosynthesis because of their role in controlling the relative ratios and amounts of dNTP pools.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RNR function.

claim: Imbalance in dNTP pools increases mutation rates, replication and repair errors, and genome instability (Hofer et al., 2012; Aye et al., 2015; Greene et al., 2020).
source: Imbalance in these pools increases mutation rates, replication and repair errors, and genome instability (Hofer et al., 2012; Aye et al., 2015; Greene et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from multiple references.

claim: Most organisms have multiple classes (designated class I, II and III) of RNRs (Nordlund and Reichard, 2006; Greene et al., 2020).
source: Most organisms have multiple classes (designated class I, II and III) (Nordlund and Reichard, 2006; Greene et al., 2020) of RNRs.
evidence: This is cited from Nordlund and Reichard, 2006 and Greene et al., 2020.

claim: All RNRs share a common active site located in a structurally homologous protein (α) and a common mechanism of NDP reduction.
source: They all share a common active site located in a structurally homologous protein (α, light and dark blue) and a common mechanism of NDP reduction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RNR structure and function.

claim: Ng possesses only one RNR, classified as a class Ia enzyme.
source: Ng possesses only one RNR, classified as a class Ia enzyme, that requires a diferric tyrosyl radical cofactor located in its subunit β (Figure 2B [orange, red], Eklund et al., 2001; Kang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis and cited references.

claim: Ng class Ia RNR requires a diferric tyrosyl radical cofactor located in its subunit β (Eklund et al., 2001; Kang et al., 2020).
source: Ng possesses only one RNR, classified as a class Ia enzyme, that requires a diferric tyrosyl radical cofactor located in its subunit β (Figure 2B [orange, red], Eklund et al., 2001; Kang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from Eklund et al., 2001 and Kang et al., 2020.

claim: Class I RNRs use α and β, two structurally homologous subunits, that are thought to form an active α2β2 complex.
source: Class I RNRs use α and β, two structurally homologous subunits, that are thought to form an active α2β2 complex (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about class I RNR structure.

claim: The α subunit contains the catalytic site (C-site) and two allosteric effector sites, one involved in the regulation of substrate specificity (S-site) and the other in general enzymatic activity (A-site) (Eriksson et al., 1997).
source: The α subunit contains the catalytic site (C-site) and two allosteric effector sites, one involved in the regulation of substrate specificity (S-site) and the other in general enzymatic activity (A-site) (Eriksson et al., 1997).
evidence: This is cited from Eriksson et al., 1997.

claim: The β subunit contains the metallo-cofactor required to initiate catalysis upon each NDP reduction event.
source: The β subunit contains the metallo-cofactor required to initiate catalysis upon each NDP reduction event.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RNR function.

claim: The metallo-cofactor in β must initiate complex reduction chemistry covering a 32 Å distance (Y122 β to C439 α) on each turnover.
source: What is most remarkable about the class Ia RNRs is that the metallo-cofactor in β must initiate complex reduction chemistry covering a 32 Å distance (Y122 β to C439 α) on each turnover (Figure 2B and E).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the radical transfer pathway in class Ia RNRs.

claim: Some of the Class Ia RNRs, including the human enzyme, can form α2β2 active structures and are known to be inhibited by dATP (Nordlund and Reichard, 2006).
source: Some of the Class Ia RNRs, including the human enzyme, can form α2β2 active structures (Figure 2B) and are known to be inhibited by dATP (Nordlund and Reichard, 2006).
evidence: This is cited from Nordlund and Reichard, 2006.

claim: The inhibited states are distinct for the Ec and human class Ia RNRs.
source: The inhibited states, however, are distinct for the Ec and human class Ia RNRs (Figure 2C and D, respectively).
evidence: This is based on structural studies showing different quaternary structures.

claim: The dATP inhibited Ec RNR forms an α4β4 ring structure where the N-terminal cone domain that binds the dATP inhibitor interacts with β2 (Ando et al., 2011; Zimanyi et al., 2012).
source: The dATP inhibited Ec RNR forms an α4β4 ring structure where the N-terminal cone domain that binds the dATP inhibitor interacts with β2 (Ando et al., 2011; Zimanyi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Ando et al., 2011 and Zimanyi et al., 2012.

claim: In the human dATP-inhibited state, the N-terminal cone domain plays a key role in formation of a trimer of α dimers in the hexameric α6 ring structure (Fairman et al., 2011; Rofougaran et al., 2006, Ando et al., 2011; Brignole et al., 2018; Greene et al., 2020).
source: In the human dATP-inhibited state, the same N-terminal cone domain (green, dotted circles in black) plays a key role in formation of a trimer of α dimers in the hexameric α6 ring structure (Fairman et al., 2011; Rofougaran et al., 2006, Ando et al., 2011; Brignole et al., 2018; Greene et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from multiple references.

claim: Both inhibited states, by distinct mechanisms, prevent long-range radical initiation between the subunits and hence NDP reduction.
source: Both inhibited states, by distinct mechanisms, prevent long-range radical initiation between the subunits and hence NDP reduction (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is inferred from structural and biochemical studies.

claim: The mutations identified in the current studies are located in the N-terminal cone domain.
source: The mutations identified in the current studies are located in the N-terminal cone domain.
evidence: This is supported by genome sequencing data.

claim: PTC-847 and PTC-672 are not active against a panel of ten Gram-negative pathogens and commensal gut microorganisms.
source: We also show that the compounds are not active against a panel of ten Gram-negative pathogens and commensal gut microorganisms.
evidence: This is supported by MIC data in Table 1B.

claim: PTC-847 and PTC-672 exhibit bactericidal activity against Ng through the inhibition of DNA synthesis.
source: Evidence is presented for bactericidal activity against Ng through the inhibition of DNA synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by time-kill curves and DNA synthesis assays.

claim: The antibacterial activity of PTC-847 and PTC-672 is not attributed to inhibition of Ng purified DNA gyrase or topoisomerase IV.
source: This activity is not attributed to inhibition of Ng purified DNA gyrase or topoisomerase IV, targets of fluoroquinolone antibiotics.
evidence: This is supported by enzyme inhibition assays showing weak or no inhibition.

claim: Using the structure of the Ec α4β4 inhibited state (Ando et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2018; Zimanyi et al., 2012), the resistant mutants map to the N-terminal cone domain of the α subunit.
source: Using the structure of the Ec α4β4 inhibited state (Ando et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2018; Zimanyi et al., 2012), we show that the resistant mutants map to the N-terminal cone domain of the α subunit (green), which interacts with the β subunit (orange) of the α4β4 inhibited RNR structure (Figures 2C and 3).
evidence: This is based on structural mapping using cited references.

claim: A high degree of sequence homology between the Ng and Ec class Ia RNRs suggested that the Ng enzyme might also form α4β4 structure.
source: A high degree of sequence homology between the Ng and Ec class Ia RNRs suggested that the Ng enzyme might also form α4β4 structure, leading us to investigate Ng RNR by negative stain EM in this study.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence homology.

claim: Ng class Ia RNR can form a dATP-induced α4β4 state.
source: Using negative stain EM analysis, we demonstrate that Ng class Ia RNR can form a dATP-induced α4β4 state and that this state is abrogated by the mutations (H25R and S41L) that cause resistance to these compounds.
evidence: This is supported by negative stain EM data in Figure 5.

claim: The dATP-induced α4β4 state is abrogated by the mutations (H25R and S41L) that cause resistance to PTC-847 and PTC-672.
source: Using negative stain EM analysis, we demonstrate that Ng class Ia RNR can form a dATP-induced α4β4 state and that this state is abrogated by the mutations (H25R and S41L) that cause resistance to these compounds.
evidence: This is supported by negative stain EM data in Figure 6.

claim: A mode of class Ia RNR inhibition by the 4-hydroxy-2-pyridones might involve binding and potentiation of an inhibited α4β4 state.
source: These studies together suggest that a mode of class Ia RNR inhibition by the 4-hydroxy-2-pyridones might involve binding and potentiation of an inhibited α4β4 state.
evidence: This is speculative based on the experimental data.

claim: When administered as a single oral dose of 60 mg/kg PTC-672, complete clearance of infections was observed with both a susceptible and an MDR strain of Ng in 10/10 mice within 24 hr following dosing.
source: When administered as a single oral dose of 60 mg/kg PTC-672, complete clearance of infections was observed with both a susceptible and an MDR strain of Ng in 10/10 mice within 24 hr following dosing.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo efficacy data in Figure 7.

claim: The H25R–α mutation reduced the competitive advantage of the susceptible and MDR Ng strains both in vitro and in vivo mixing experiments.
source: We also showed that the H25R–α mutation reduced the competitive advantage of the susceptible and MDR Ng strains both in vitro and in vivo mixing experiments.
evidence: This is supported by fitness testing data in Figures 8 and 9.

claim: Treatment with PTC-847, PTC-672 or related analogs exhibiting an acceptable safety profile may be more selective, better tolerated, and lessen the emergence of resistance compared with current therapies.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that treatment with PTC-847, PTC-672 or related analogs exhibiting an acceptable safety profile may be more selective, better tolerated, and lessen the emergence of resistance compared with current therapies.
evidence: This is speculative based on the experimental data.

claim: PTC-847 exhibited potent antibacterial activity against all six Ng strains with MICs ranging from 0.05 to 0.1 µg/mL.
source: PTC-847 exhibited potent antibacterial activity against all six Ng strains with MICs ranging from 0.05 to 0.1 µg/mL.
evidence: This is supported by MIC data in Table 1A.

claim: PTC-847 exhibited a MIC of 0.2 µg/mL against the weakly immunogenic NMSB strain.
source: The weakly immunogenic NMSB strain had a MIC of 0.2 µg/mL (Table 1A).
evidence: This is supported by MIC data in Table 1A.

claim: PTC-672 exhibited MICs ranging from 0.05 to 0.4 µg/mL against the six Ng strains.
source: PTC-672 exhibited MICs ranging from 0.05 to 0.4 µg/mL against the six Ng strains, and a MIC of 0.1 µg/mL against the NMSB strain (Table 1A).
evidence: This is supported by MIC data in Table 1A.

claim: PTC-672 exhibited a MIC of 0.1 µg/mL against the NMSB strain.
source: PTC-672 exhibited MICs ranging from 0.05 to 0.4 µg/mL against the six Ng strains, and a MIC of 0.1 µg/mL against the NMSB strain (Table 1A).
evidence: This is supported by MIC data in Table 1A.

claim: PTC-565 exhibited antibacterial activity against a broad spectrum of Gram-negative pathogens.
source: The compound PTC-565 representing the [5,6] fused ring structure (Figure 1A) exhibited antibacterial activity against a broad spectrum of Gram-negative pathogens (Table 1A and B); in contrast, PTC-847 and PTC-672 are inactive against the panel of Gram-negative pathogens and normal gut organisms evidenced by MICs ranging from 12.5 to ≥62.5 µg/mL (Table 1B).
evidence: This is supported by MIC data in Table 1.

claim: PTC-847 and PTC-672 are inactive against the panel of Gram-negative pathogens and normal gut organisms evidenced by MICs ranging from 12.5 to ≥62.5 µg/mL.
source: The compound PTC-565 representing the [5,6] fused ring structure (Figure 1A) exhibited antibacterial activity against a broad spectrum of Gram-negative pathogens (Table 1A and B); in contrast, PTC-847 and PTC-672 are inactive against the panel of Gram-negative pathogens and normal gut organisms evidenced by MICs ranging from 12.5 to ≥62.5 µg/mL (Table 1B).
evidence: This is supported by MIC data in Table 1B.

claim: Susceptibility testing resulted in MIC90 values for PTC-847 and PTC-672 equal to 0.12 µg/mL against a panel of 206 Ng strains with broad resistance phenotypes.
source: Susceptibility testing resulted in MIC90 values for PTC-847 and PTC-672 equal to 0.12 µg/mL (determined from values in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by MIC data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: At concentrations of 1 X MIC or greater, PTC-847 and PTC-672 exhibit time-dependent cidality against the Ng 13477 strain.
source: At concentrations of 1 X MIC or greater, PTC-847 and PTC-672 exhibit time-dependent cidality against the Ng 13477 strain (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by time-kill curve data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: A time-dependent post antibiotic effect was observed with PTC-847.
source: In addition, a time-dependent post antibiotic effect was observed with PTC-847.
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Suppression of bacterial growth persisted even after the removal of PTC-847.
source: Suppression of bacterial growth persisted even after the removal of PTC-847 (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Inhibition of DNA but not protein synthesis appears to be responsible for growth inhibition by PTC-847.
source: The results revealed that inhibition of DNA but not protein synthesis appears to be responsible for growth inhibition by PTC-847 (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by radiolabeled precursor incorporation assays in Supplementary file 4.

claim: The PTC-847 IC50 value for Ng gyrase was 19 µM and >32 µM for Ng topoisomerase IV.
source: The PTC-847 half maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) value for Ng gyrase was 19 µM and >32 µM for Ng topoisomerase IV and both Ec topoisomerases (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by enzyme inhibition assay data in Table 2.

claim: PTC-847 IC50 was >32 µM for both Ec topoisomerases.
source: The PTC-847 half maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) value for Ng gyrase was 19 µM and >32 µM for Ng topoisomerase IV and both Ec topoisomerases (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by enzyme inhibition assay data in Table 2.

claim: PTC-847 at 100 μM did not appreciably inhibit the activity of human topoisomerase II.
source: Furthermore, PTC-847 at 100 μM did not appreciably inhibit the activity of human topoisomerase II.
evidence: This is supported by enzyme inhibition assay data in Table 2.

claim: Ciprofloxacin showed IC50 values ranging from 0.4 to 18 µM against topoisomerases.
source: As a control, the fluoroquinolone antibiotic ciprofloxacin showed IC50 values ranging from 0.4 to 18 µM (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by enzyme inhibition assay data in Table 2.

claim: Topoisomerases are not the primary targets for PTC-847 in Ng.
source: These findings together suggest that topoisomerases are not the primary targets for PTC-847 in Ng.
evidence: This is inferred from the weak inhibition of topoisomerases.

claim: The frequency of resistance for PTC-847R at 4 x the MIC was 3.6 × 10–8.
source: The frequency of resistance for PTC-847R at 4 x the MIC was 3.6 × 10–8, compared to ciprofloxacin at 1.2 × 10–8 and ceftriaxone at 7.7 × 10–9 under identical conditions.
evidence: This is supported by resistance selection experiments.

claim: The frequency of resistance for ciprofloxacin at 4 x the MIC was 1.2 × 10–8.
source: The frequency of resistance for PTC-847R at 4 x the MIC was 3.6 × 10–8, compared to ciprofloxacin at 1.2 × 10–8 and ceftriaxone at 7.7 × 10–9 under identical conditions.
evidence: This is supported by resistance selection experiments.

claim: The frequency of resistance for ceftriaxone at 4 x the MIC was 7.7 × 10–9.
source: The frequency of resistance for PTC-847R at 4 x the MIC was 3.6 × 10–8, compared to ciprofloxacin at 1.2 × 10–8 and ceftriaxone at 7.7 × 10–9 under identical conditions.
evidence: This is supported by resistance selection experiments.

claim: The PTC-847R strain was as sensitive to all classes of antibiotics as the wild-type Ng 13477 strain, except for susceptibility to PTC-847.
source: The PTC-847R strain was as sensitive to all classes of antibiotics as the wild-type Ng 13477 strain, except for susceptibility to PTC-847.
evidence: This is supported by antibiotic susceptibility testing in Supplementary file 6.

claim: The MIC for PTC-847 against Ng 13477 was 0.05 µg/mL compared to 15.6 µg/mL for the PTC-847R isolate.
source: The MIC for PTC-847 against Ng 13477 was 0.05 µg/mL compared to 15.6 µg/mL for the PTC-847R isolate.
evidence: This is supported by MIC data.

claim: A single C to T transition that results in a serine (S) to leucine (L) amino acid substitution at position 41 (S41L) in the α-subunit of the Ng class Ia RNR was identified in the PTC-847R isolate.
source: A single C to T transition that results in a serine (S) to leucine (L) amino acid substitution at position 41 (S41L) in the α-subunit of the Ng class Ia RNR was identified (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by whole genome sequencing data.

claim: Sequencing the PTC-672R class Ia RNR gene revealed a single A to G transition that resulted in a histidine (H) to arginine (R) amino acid substitution at position 25 (H25R) in the α-subunit.
source: Sequencing the PTC-672R class Ia RNR gene revealed a single A to G transition that resulted in a histidine (H) to arginine (R) amino acid substitution at position 25 (H25R) in the α-subunit (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by whole genome sequencing data.

claim: An increased ratio of NTPs to dNTPs in the susceptible WT 13477 strain was observed upon treatment with PTC-847 at 1 x MIC for 1 hr.
source: In support of the mechanism of inhibition of PTC-847, an increased ratio of NTPs to dNTPs in the susceptible WT 13477 strain was observed upon treatment with the inhibitor at 1 x MIC for 1 hr followed by nucleotide extraction and LC/MS analysis (Chen et al., 2009; Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is supported by LC/MS analysis of nucleotide pools in Supplementary file 7.

claim: The activity of Ng RNR at 0.1 µM and 1:1(α:β) ratio of subunits was 1300 nmol min–1 mg–1 with GDP/TTP as substrate and effector.
source: The activity at 0.1 µM and 1:1(α:β) ratio of subunits was 1300 nmol min–1 mg–1 with GDP/TTP as substrate and effector, similar to that for Ec RNR (2500 nmol min–1 mg–1 with CDP/ATP as substrate and effector; Materials and methods, Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is supported by enzyme activity assays in Supplementary file 8.

claim: The activity of Ec RNR was 2500 nmol min–1 mg–1 with CDP/ATP as substrate and effector.
source: The activity at 0.1 µM and 1:1(α:β) ratio of subunits was 1300 nmol min–1 mg–1 with GDP/TTP as substrate and effector, similar to that for Ec RNR (2500 nmol min–1 mg–1 with CDP/ATP as substrate and effector; Materials and methods, Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is supported by enzyme activity assays.

claim: The apparent Km is 0.03 µM for Ng RNR.
source: The apparent Km is 0.03 µM for Ng RNR and as noted above that for Ec and human RNRs is ~0.2 µM.
evidence: This is supported by enzyme kinetic assays.

claim: The apparent Km for Ec and human RNRs is ~0.2 µM.
source: The apparent Km is 0.03 µM for Ng RNR and as noted above that for Ec and human RNRs is ~0.2 µM.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ec and human RNR kinetics.

claim: Studies of Ng RNR activity as a function of dATP concentration reveal a profile very similar to Ec RNR, including biphasic kinetics based on dATP binding to both the S-site and A-site (Hofer et al., 2012).
source: Studies of Ng RNR activity as a function of dATP concentration (Supplementary file 9) reveal a profile very similar to Ec RNR, including biphasic kinetics based on dATP binding to both the S-site and A-site (Hofer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by enzyme inhibition assays in Supplementary file 9 and cited from Hofer et al., 2012.

claim: There is 76% sequence identity for α between Ng and Ec.
source: This result is expected given the 76% sequence identity for α between Ng and Ec, including the H25 and S41 (Figure 3) found altered in Ng resistant to the PTC compounds.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Human α shares only 30% sequence identity to Ng.
source: Human α, on the other hand, shares only 30% sequence identity to Ng and does not have residues homologous to either H25 or S41.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Human α does not have residues homologous to either H25 or S41 of Ng α.
source: Human α, on the other hand, shares only 30% sequence identity to Ng and does not have residues homologous to either H25 or S41.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Inhibition studies with H25R and S41L Ngα mutants showed much lower sensitivity to dATP.
source: Inhibition studies with H25R and S41L Ngα mutants showed much lower sensitivity to dATP (Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This is supported by enzyme inhibition assays in Supplementary file 9.

claim: The Ec RNR is inhibited by PTC-847 and PTC-672.
source: As expected, based on sequence similarity, the Ec RNR is also inhibited, whereas the human enzyme, even at 100 μM inhibitor concentration, still retains substantial activity (Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by enzyme inhibition assays in Table 3.

claim: The human RNR, even at 100 μM inhibitor concentration, still retains substantial activity.
source: As expected, based on sequence similarity, the Ec RNR is also inhibited, whereas the human enzyme, even at 100 μM inhibitor concentration, still retains substantial activity (Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by enzyme inhibition assays in Table 3.

claim: Inhibition of Ng RNR is enhanced in the presence of allosteric inhibitor dATP.
source: Inhibition of Ng RNR is enhanced in the presence of allosteric inhibitor dATP (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that in vivo, PTC-847 and PTC-672 could act by stabilizing a dATP-induced inhibited state of Ng RNR.
evidence: This is supported by enzyme inhibition assays in Figure 4.

claim: In vivo, PTC-847 and PTC-672 could act by stabilizing a dATP-induced inhibited state of Ng RNR.
source: Inhibition of Ng RNR is enhanced in the presence of allosteric inhibitor dATP (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that in vivo, PTC-847 and PTC-672 could act by stabilizing a dATP-induced inhibited state of Ng RNR.
evidence: This is speculative based on the in vitro data.

claim: In the presence of 1 mM dATP, ring structures are present in Ng RNR samples.
source: Panel A shows that, in the presence of 1 mM dATP, ring structures are present.
evidence: This is supported by negative stain EM images in Figure 5A.

claim: Ng Ia RNR, like the Ec enzyme, forms the α4β4 ring structure inhibited state induced by dATP.
source: The 2D classifications and 3D reconstruction are shown in Figure 5B and C, and reveal that Ng Ia RNR, like the Ec enzyme, forms the α4β4 ring structure inhibited state induced by dATP.
evidence: This is supported by negative stain EM data in Figure 5.

claim: In the WT control, α4β4 ring structures are clearly visible whereas no such structures are observed with either H25R or S41L mutant.
source: As shown in Figure 6, in the WT control, α4β4 ring structures are clearly visible whereas no such structures are observed with either mutant.
evidence: This is supported by negative stain EM images in Figure 6.

claim: No α4β4 structures are observed for either the WT or mutant proteins when ATP (an activator) replaces the dATP inhibitor.
source: An additional control in which ATP (an activator) replaces the dATP inhibitor, also reveals no α4β4 structures for either the WT or mutant proteins (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from control experiments.

claim: PTC-672 is far less effective at inhibiting H25R and S41L RNR variants than it is at inhibiting WT Ng RNR.
source: We pursued this idea and found that PTC-672 is far less effective at inhibiting these RNR variants than it is at inhibiting WT Ng RNR (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by enzyme inhibition assays in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A significant amount of inhibition is still occurring with PTC-672 against H25R and S41L variants.
source: However, a significant amount of inhibition is still occurring (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), especially compared to the substantial loss of inhibition for dATP for RNR variants (Supplementary file 9) that cannot form rings.
evidence: This is supported by enzyme inhibition assays in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: PTC-672, and likely PTC-847, has more than one mode of RNR inhibition.
source: This comparison suggests that PTC-672, and likely PTC-847 (not tested), has more than one mode of RNR inhibition.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that inhibition persists in mutants that cannot form rings.

claim: There is an increase in the number of α4β4 rings in the presence of PTC-672/GDP/TTP compared to GDP/TTP alone.
source: Using mass photometry to evaluate oligomeric states (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Figure 6—figure supplement 3), we find an increase in the number of α4β4 rings in the presence of PTC-672/GDP/TTP compared to GDP/TTP alone, but fewer rings than in the dATP control (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by mass photometry data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and 3.

claim: For PTC-847, no increase in rings is observed by mass photometry.
source: For PTC-847, no increase in rings is observed (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by mass photometry data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and 3.

claim: In vivo, PTC-672/PTC-847 are not binding to the dATP site in the cone domain and inducing the conformational changes necessary for α4β4 formation but rather acting synergistically with dATP.
source: Based on these results and on the finding that PTC compounds potentiate the inhibitory effects of dATP (Figure 4), we postulate that in vivo, PTC-672/PTC-847 are not binding to the dATP site in the cone domain and inducing the conformational changes necessary for α4β4 formation but rather acting synergistically with dATP.
evidence: This is speculative based on the experimental data.

claim: PTC-847 and PTC-672 spared the commensal bacteria relative to the control antibiotic solithromycin.
source: PTC-847 and PTC-672 spared the commensal bacteria relative to the control antibiotic solithromycin (Supplementary file 10), a fourth-generation macrolide with enhanced activity against macrolide-resistant bacteria (Farrell et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by MIC data in Supplementary file 10.

claim: PTC-672's effect on two commensal Neisseria strains was inhibited, but to a lesser extent (approximately 10-fold) than that of Ng.
source: Furthermore, PTC-672's effect on two commensal Neisseria strains was also assessed. These isolates were inhibited, but to a lesser extent (approximately 10-fold) than that of Ng (Supplementary file 11).
evidence: This is supported by MIC data in Supplementary file 11.

claim: Treatment with a single oral dose of ciprofloxacin at 30 mg/kg resulted in complete clearance of the Iso 13477 StrepR infection in 10/10 mice within 24 hr following treatment.
source: Treatment with a single oral dose of ciprofloxacin at 30 mg/kg resulted in complete clearance of the infection in 10/10 mice (~4 log drop in bacterial infection) within 24 hr following treatment.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo efficacy data in Figure 7A.

claim: PTC-672 administered as a single oral dose (10, 15, 20, 25, or 30 mg/kg) resulted in clearance of Iso 13477 StrepR infection at all doses in 10/10 mice within 24 hr.
source: PTC-672 administered as a single oral dose (10, 15, 20, 25, or 30 mg/kg) resulted in clearance of infection at all doses in 10/10 mice within 24 hr.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo efficacy data in Figure 7A.

claim: The clearance of Iso 13477 StrepR infection by ciprofloxacin or PTC-672 was sustained through Day 7.
source: The clearance of infection by ciprofloxacin or PTC-672 was sustained through Day 7.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo efficacy data in Figure 7A.

claim: Treatment with a single intraperitoneal dose of ceftriaxone (100 mg/kg) resulted in complete clearance of the Iso 13479 StrepR infection in 10/10 mice within 24 hr.
source: Treatment with a single intraperitoneal dose of ceftriaxone (100 mg/kg) resulted in complete clearance of the infection in 10/10 mice within 24 hr and clearance of infection was sustained until Day 7.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo efficacy data in Figure 7B.

claim: PTC-672 administered as a single oral dose (60 mg/kg) resulted in complete clearance of the Iso 13479 StrepR infection in 10/10 mice within 24 hr of dosing.
source: PTC-672 administered as a single oral dose (60 mg/kg) resulted in complete clearance of the infection in 10/10 mice within 24 hr of dosing and was also sustained until Day 7.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo efficacy data in Figure 7B.

claim: At the lower dose of 30 mg/kg PTC-672 resulted in an average 1.46-log drop in bacterial load (8/9 mice cleared infection) 24 hr post-dose in the Iso 13479 StrepR model.
source: At the lower dose of 30 mg/kg PTC-672 resulted in an average 1.46-log drop in bacterial load (8/9 mice cleared infection) 24 hr post-dose.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo efficacy data in Figure 7B.

claim: Infection in several mice re-bounded on subsequent days of the study at 30 mg/kg PTC-672 suggesting that a dose of 30 mg/kg was sub-efficacious in the Iso 13479 StrepR model.
source: However, infection in several mice re-bounded on subsequent days of the study suggesting that a dose of 30 mg/kg was sub-efficacious in the Iso 13479 StrepR model.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo efficacy data in Figure 7B.

claim: The CI for Ng Iso 13477 StrepR-PTC-672H25R and Iso 13479 StrepR-PTC-672H25R decreased exponentially to a CI of 0.06 at 8 hr.
source: In this experiment, the CI for Ng Iso 13477 StrepR-PTC-672H25R and Iso 13479 StrepR-PTC-672H25R decreased exponentially to a CI of 0.06 at 8 hr (Figure 8), demonstrating that the H25R engineered resistant bacteria are less fit for competitive infection with their respective parent strains while the isolates had similar in vitro doubling times.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro fitness testing data in Figure 8.

claim: The H25R engineered resistant bacteria are less fit for competitive infection with their respective parent strains while the isolates had similar in vitro doubling times.
source: In this experiment, the CI for Ng Iso 13477 StrepR-PTC-672H25R and Iso 13479 StrepR-PTC-672H25R decreased exponentially to a CI of 0.06 at 8 hr (Figure 8), demonstrating that the H25R engineered resistant bacteria are less fit for competitive infection with their respective parent strains while the isolates had similar in vitro doubling times.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro fitness testing data in Figure 8.

claim: When infected with only the Iso 13477 StrepR-PTC-672H25R or the Iso 13479 StrepR-PTC-672H25R strain, the infection was similar to that elicited with the StrepR parent strain.
source: When infected with only the Iso 13477 StrepR-PTC-672H25R or the Iso 13479 StrepR-PTC-672H25R strain, the infection was similar to that elicited with the StrepR parent strain.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo infection data.

claim: For fitness testing with mixed strains, the mean and median CIs for Ng Iso StrepR-PTC-672H25R 13477 and Iso 13479 StrepR-PTC-672H25R resistant strains decreased to <0.01 by Day 2 post-infection.
source: For fitness testing with mixed strains, the mean and median CIs for Ng Iso StrepR-PTC-672H25R 13477 and Iso 13479 StrepR-PTC-672H25R resistant strains decreased to <0.01 by Day 2 post-infection (Figure 9).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo fitness testing data in Figure 9.

claim: Although the PTC-672-resistant Ng strains infection levels in mice were comparable to those for the isogenic PTC-672 susceptible parent strains, when the two isogenic strains were inoculated in the same anatomical location in vivo, the PTC-672-resistant isolates did not successfully compete with the parent strains.
source: Thus, although the PTC-672-resistant Ng strains infection levels in mice were comparable to those for the isogenic PTC-672 susceptible parent strains, when the two isogenic strains were inoculated in the same anatomical location in vivo, the PTC-672-resistant isolates did not successfully compete with the parent strains.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo fitness testing data in Figure 9.

claim: If PTC-672 resistance does arise in Ng strains in situ, the PTC-672 resistant strain would be at a competitive disadvantage and thus less likely to propagate.
source: These data suggest that if PTC-672 resistance does arise in Ng strains in situ, the PTC-672 resistant strain would be at a competitive disadvantage and thus less likely to propagate.
evidence: This is inferred from the fitness testing data.

claim: PTC-672 may lessen the emergence of resistance compared with current therapies.
source: These results combined with the outcomes of the in vitro fitness study suggest that PTC-672 may lessen the emergence of resistance compared with current therapies.
evidence: This is speculative based on the fitness testing data.

claim: The discovery that the 4-hydroxy-2-pyridone compounds with 5,6 fused ring structures (Gerasyuto et al., 2016) exhibited broad-spectrum bactericidal activity against many Gram-negative pathogens by targeting topoisomerases and inhibiting DNA synthesis.
source: The discovery that the 4-hydroxy-2-pyridone compounds with 5,6 fused ring structures (Gerasyuto et al., 2016) exhibited broad-spectrum bactericidal activity against many Gram-negative pathogens by targeting topoisomerases and inhibiting DNA synthesis provided the impetus for further investigation of a general pharmacophore.
evidence: This is cited from Gerasyuto et al., 2016.

claim: The discovery that the 4,5-fused pyridines with indolyl and imidazolyl moiety rings were potent and selective inhibitors of Ng, Nm, and MDR Ng led to further studies to identify the target(s) of these compounds.
source: The discovery that the 4,5-fused pyridines with indolyl and imidazolyl moiety rings (Figure 1B and C) were potent and selective inhibitors of Ng, Nm, and MDR Ng (Table 1) led to further studies to identify the target(s) of these compounds and the suitability of two compounds (PTC-847 and PTC-672) as potential single organism therapeutics.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: These compounds, although inhibiting DNA synthesis, do not appear to target Ng gyrase or topoisomerase IV, but rather uniquely target Ng Ia RNR.
source: We demonstrated that these compounds, although inhibiting DNA synthesis, do not appear to target Ng gyrase or topoisomerase IV, but rather uniquely target Ng Ia RNR.
evidence: This is supported by enzyme inhibition assays and resistance mapping.

claim: The dramatic increase in life threatening bacterial infections, coupled to the increase in resistance and MDR to widely used therapeutics (Walsh, 2015) makes identification of this new therapeutic target particularly exciting.
source: The dramatic increase in life threatening bacterial infections, coupled to the increase in resistance and MDR to widely used therapeutics (Walsh, 2015) makes identification of this new therapeutic target particularly exciting.
evidence: This is cited from Walsh, 2015.

claim: Studies in vitro (Chen et al., 2018) and in vivo (Ahluwalia et al., 2012) of Ec RNR establish that substitutions of α/β interface residues H23 and S39 (H25 and S41 in Ng RNR) disrupt this quaternary structure.
source: Studies in vitro (Chen et al., 2018) and in vivo (Ahluwalia et al., 2012) of Ec RNR establish that substitutions of α/β interface residues H23 and S39 (H25 and S41 in Ng RNR) disrupt this quaternary structure and our preliminary data obtained using EM suggest the same is true for Ng RNR (Figure 5).
evidence: This is cited from Chen et al., 2018 and Ahluwalia et al., 2012.

claim: Trapping distinct quaternary structures of regulatory proteins with small molecule inhibitors has been successfully exploited with identification of the importance of inhibited protein kinase states in targeting signaling pathways involved in the regulation of cancer cell growth (Greene et al., 2020).
source: Trapping distinct quaternary structures of regulatory proteins with small molecule inhibitors has been successfully exploited with identification of the importance of inhibited protein kinase states in targeting signaling pathways involved in the regulation of cancer cell growth (Greene et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from Greene et al., 2020.

claim: Biochemical and cell-culture studies have revealed that clorfarabine (ClF), a nucleoside therapeutic used in the treatment of acute lymphoblastic and acute myeloid leukemias, subsequent to its phosphorylation to a di- or trinucleotide (ClFDP, ClFTP) binds to the α subunit of human Ia RNR and potentiates formation of the α6 inhibited state (Aye and Stubbe, 2011; Brignole et al., 2018).
source: Recently, biochemical and cell-culture studies have revealed that clorfarabine (ClF), a nucleoside therapeutic used in the treatment of acute lymphoblastic and acute myeloid leukemias, subsequent to its phosphorylation to a di- or trinucleotide (ClFDP, ClFTP) binds to the α subunit of human Ia RNR and potentiates formation of the α6 inhibited state (Aye and Stubbe, 2011; Brignole et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from Aye and Stubbe, 2011 and Brignole et al., 2018.

claim: In contrast with the dATP-induced α6 inhibited state (Fairman et al., 2011), which rapidly reverts to a mixture of α monomers and dimers on dATP dissociation, both the ClFDP and ClFTP α6 states remain hexameric for some time subsequent to their dissociation (Brignole et al., 2018; Aye and Stubbe, 2011).
source: In contrast with the dATP-induced α6 inhibited state (Fairman et al., 2011), which rapidly reverts to a mixture of α monomers and dimers on dATP dissociation, both the ClFDP and ClFTP α6 states remain hexameric for some time subsequent to their dissociation (Brignole et al., 2018; Aye and Stubbe, 2011).
evidence: This is cited from multiple references.

claim: The E. coli Ia RNR, which does not form an α6 state, is not inhibited by ClFTP.
source: Interestingly the E. coli Ia RNR, which does not form an α6 state, is not inhibited by ClFTP.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ec RNR.

claim: Despite the structural homology between Ng and human α, no appreciable inhibition of the human RNR by PTC-847 or PTC-672 is observed.
source: Despite the structural homology between Ng and human α, no appreciable inhibition of the human RNR by PTC-847 or PTC-672 is observed (Table 3), consistent with the distinct α6 quaternary structure.
evidence: This is supported by enzyme inhibition assays in Table 3.

claim: The discovery that PTC-847 and PTC-672 inhibited Ng but not human Ia RNR suggests that trapping the inhibited quaternary state might be a new approach for therapeutics that selectively target Ng.
source: The discovery that PTC-847 and PTC-672 inhibited Ng but not human Ia RNR suggests that trapping the inhibited quaternary state might be a new approach for therapeutics that selectively target Ng.
evidence: This is speculative based on the experimental data.

claim: This selectivity may be explained by the observation that Ng and Nm possess only a single RNR, whereas many microorganisms have multiple RNRs.
source: We postulate that this selectivity may be explained by the observation that Ng and Nm possess only a single RNR, whereas many microorganisms, including Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Bacillus subtilis, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Bacteroides fragilis, Clostridium difficile, Lactobacillus gasseri, and Fusobacterium nucleatum, have multiple RNRs (additional class Is [Ib-Ie] or class II and III) (Lundin et al., 2009; Stubbe and Seyedsayamdost, 2018) that may not be targeted by these compounds (Supplementary file 12).
evidence: This is speculative based on genomic analysis and cited references.

claim: Based on the demonstrated target and biological selectivity of PTC-847 and PTC-672, these compounds may be better tolerated compared with current therapies.
source: Based on the demonstrated target and biological selectivity of PTC-847 and PTC-672, these compounds may be better tolerated compared with current therapies.
evidence: This is speculative based on the selectivity data.

claim: A recent study examined the cost effectiveness of a novel, pathogen-specific agent targeting carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii (CRAB) in comparison with the standard-of-care (Spellberg and Rex, 2013).
source: A recent study examined the cost effectiveness of a novel, pathogen-specific agent targeting carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii (CRAB) in comparison with the standard-of-care (Spellberg and Rex, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Spellberg and Rex, 2013.

claim: The analysis based on annual incidence of sensitive versus resistant infections, cost of treatments, and mortality of infections showed that a single-pathogen agent could provide benefit at a cost well below the traditional benchmarks used to define cost effective therapy.
source: The analysis based on annual incidence of sensitive versus resistant infections, cost of treatments, and mortality of infections showed that a single-pathogen agent could provide benefit at a cost well below the traditional benchmarks used to define cost effective therapy.
evidence: This is cited from Spellberg and Rex, 2013.

claim: Our compounds fit the profile for a cost-effective single pathogen treatment paradigm for Ng.
source: Our compounds fit the profile for a cost-effective single pathogen treatment paradigm for Ng.
evidence: This is speculative based on the selectivity and efficacy data.
